questions.q: What is Alison's basic claim about the dramatic arc?
choices: It is one pattern among many, treated as the only one
questions.explain: She doesn't reject the arc, only its monopoly.

questions.q: Where does Alison look for alternative shapes?
questions.explain: Meanders, spirals, wavelets, cells, networks, explosions.

questions.q: A memoir keeps returning to the night of a fire, each time with more understanding. Which pattern is it?
questions.explain: A spiral circles the same center at deepening levels.

questions.q: A novel is told through eight characters, each section showing the same wedding from a different side. Which pattern fits best?
questions.explain: Pieces arranged around a central point, like spokes around a hub.

questions.q: What does Alison mean by shifting attention from plot to design?
choices: Noticing the felt shape of a text, its repetitions, motifs and arrangement, as a source of momentum
questions.explain: Pattern can pull readers along as strongly as 'what happens next?'

questions.q: A long-running series ripples along through many small rises and falls rather than building to one peak. Which of Alison's patterns describes it?
questions.explain: Wavelets are many small tensions and releases instead of one great wave.

questions.q: What's a common criticism of Meander, Spiral, Explode?
choices: Its natural images are evocative but don't always show how to sustain a long work
questions.explain: Critics note that metaphors aren't mechanics, especially over the length of a novel or film.

ideas: Narratives can borrow their shapes from nature: rivers that meander, shells that spiral, cells that divide.
A story can ripple through many small rises and falls instead of building one great wave.
Readers are pattern-seekers, and design can pull them through a text as strongly as suspense.
